modules.title: Why we run an ISMS
modules.summary: How ISO 27001 connects to your day-to-day work.
modules.body:
An ISMS (Information Security Management System) is the framework we use to keep customer data, source code, and our own internal records safe. ISO 27001 is the international standard that an external auditor reviews us against. We are not running an ISMS to please auditors — we run one because losing customer trust is the fastest way to lose customers.

In practice the ISMS shows up as policies in CloudAnzen, evidence we collect during normal work, and short reviews we do every quarter. Your part is recognising that the controls you follow (Slack approval requests, ticket discipline, change reviews) are what the ISMS actually IS.

When an auditor visits, they sample real evidence: a Jira ticket, a Slack thread, a screenshot. The ISMS doesn't have a separate filing cabinet — your everyday work is the cabinet.
bullets: The ISMS is the controls you already follow during normal work.
Auditors sample real artefacts — tickets, Slack threads, screenshots.
Reporting concerns early is faster than backfilling evidence later.
Every team contributes to evidence quality, not just the security team.
When in doubt, ask in #security — silence costs more than questions.

questions.prompt: When an external ISO 27001 auditor visits, what do they look at most?

choices.label: Marketing decks describing our security program.
Real, dated evidence from our normal workflows (tickets, Slack, change reviews).
A separate "audit binder" the compliance team prepares the week before.
Conversations with executives only.

questions.prompt: Which of these are part of "the ISMS" in practice? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: The change-management ticket where a deploy was approved.
A Slack request asking your manager for access.
Our quarterly access review spreadsheet.
The policy PDF sitting unread in a Drive folder.

questions.prompt: What is the best first move?

choices.label: Stay quiet — the email is redacted, so it is probably fine.
Flag it in #security with the link so the team can confirm whether it is in policy.
DM the teammate to delete it; mention nothing to security.
Take a screenshot and post it in a separate channel for later discussion.

questions.scenario: You spot a teammate sharing a customer screenshot in a public #demo channel. It has a customer name + a redacted email. You're not sure if it crosses a line.

modules.title: Access + identity
modules.summary: MFA, password manager, least privilege, access reviews.
modules.body:
Most security incidents start with credentials. A teammate's password ends up in a breach corpus, an attacker logs in, and from there they're a "valid user" — which is the hardest kind of attacker to detect.

We push hard on three habits: every account behind a password manager + MFA, least-privilege access (you have what your role needs, nothing more), and quarterly access reviews to catch creeping permissions. These three habits prevent more breaches than any fancy tooling.

When you change role or leave a project, your access should change too. If you notice a teammate still in a Slack channel or repo they no longer need, that's a real audit finding waiting to happen. Flag it in #access-management.
bullets: Every login goes through the password manager — never reuse passwords.
MFA on every account, every time. If a prompt surprises you, deny + report.
Ask for least privilege — narrower scope is faster to get approved and easier to defend.
Quarterly access reviews are real — answer them seriously.
Role change = access change. Flag stale access when you spot it.

questions.prompt: Which of these signals point at credential compromise? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: You get an MFA prompt you did not trigger.
A login alert says you signed in from a country you have never visited.
A password manager warning that one of your saved logins appeared in a breach.
Slack told you your status was set to "active" this morning.

questions.prompt: A teammate asks for production database read access "just in case they need to debug something next sprint". What is the right response?

choices.label: Grant standing read access — it is only read.
Decline outright; debugging is not their job.
Offer just-in-time scoped access for the sprint, with auto-expiry and a request trail.
Share your own credentials so they can debug under your account.

questions.prompt: What should you do? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Deny the MFA prompt.
Report the unexpected prompt in #security (or page the on-call).
Approve it once just to clear the notification.
Rotate your password through the password manager.

questions.scenario: It is 11pm and your phone buzzes with an MFA approval prompt to log in to Okta. You did not start a login. The prompt has the right name and the right look.

modules.title: Device hygiene
modules.summary: Managed laptops, screen lock, BYOD limits, lost device.
modules.body:
Your laptop is a customer-data device. The MDM (mobile device management) enrolment that you went through during onboarding gives the security team the ability to push patches, lock a lost device, and confirm disk encryption is on. It is not surveillance — it is the seatbelt.

Three habits matter most: lock the screen every time you step away (Cmd+Ctrl+Q on macOS, Win+L on Windows), keep the OS + browser updated within a week of release, and report a lost or stolen device within the hour. The faster we lock and wipe, the smaller the blast radius.

BYOD (personal devices) and managed devices have different rules. If you can avoid touching customer data from a personal device, do — we have managed devices for a reason.
bullets: Lock the screen every single time you step away.
Take OS + browser updates within a week of release.
Lost or stolen device → #security within the hour.
Customer data stays on managed devices when possible.
Never disable the MDM agent or disk encryption.

questions.prompt: You realise on the train home that your work laptop is no longer in your bag. What is the right first action?

choices.label: Wait until morning to see if it turns up.
Contact #security / on-call now so MDM can lock + wipe.
Buy a new laptop and restore from your personal iCloud.
DM your manager only.

questions.prompt: Which of these are acceptable on your CloudAnzen managed laptop? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Installing a productivity app from the company-approved software catalog.
Signing into your personal Dropbox / personal Google Drive on the device.
Installing a browser extension you found on a Reddit thread.
Using the password manager + MFA app the company set up.

questions.prompt: What do you tell them?

choices.label: Sure, just turn it back on after the launch.
Tell them to open an IT ticket so the agent can be tuned, and keep MDM on.
Show them the shortcut to uninstall the agent.
Ignore the question.

questions.scenario: A teammate complains that the MDM agent on their laptop is slowing things down and asks if they can disable it for a few days while they finish a launch.

modules.title: Data classification + handling
modules.summary: Internal, confidential, customer — and how each is handled.
modules.body:
Everything we touch falls into a sensitivity bucket: Public (marketing), Internal (most Notion pages, design docs), Confidential (security plans, internal financials, customer lists), and Customer Data (anything our customers gave us).

The bucket determines who can see it, where it can be stored, how it can be shared, and how long we keep it. Customer Data is the strictest — it stays in our approved customer systems (the product, the data warehouse with row-level access) and never gets pasted into chats, AI tools, or personal drives.

If you are about to share something and you cannot quickly say which bucket it lives in, pause and ask. The pause is cheaper than a leak.
bullets: Customer Data → approved systems only, never in chat, AI, or personal drive.
Confidential → internal channels with documented audience.
Internal → default for most company work.
Public → marketing or trust-center material that already cleared review.
Cannot place the bucket? Pause and ask in #security.

questions.prompt: A customer success teammate asks you to paste a customer's support transcript into ChatGPT to summarise. The transcript has the customer's name and a vendor name. What is the right answer?

choices.label: Paste it in — summarisation is harmless.
Use the company-approved AI workflow or aggressively redact first.
Redact only the customer name; leave the rest.
Refuse to help.

questions.prompt: Rank these places to share a Confidential incident postmortem from MOST to LEAST appropriate.

choices.label: A #security-incidents Slack channel with documented membership.
A DM with the on-call engineer for context only.
The company-wide #general Slack channel.
Your personal Google Drive for safekeeping.

questions.prompt: Which of these count as Customer Data under our classification policy? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: A support ticket transcript including the customer's admin email.
An OAuth token the customer issued for our Slack integration.
A G2 testimonial the customer already published.
An auditor's finding against the customer's ISMS.

modules.title: Phishing + social engineering
modules.summary: Spot it, report it, do not engage.
modules.body:
Phishing is the most common way attackers get into companies our size. Modern phishing is competent: clean grammar, real logos, and the email even references a real coworker. The tells are subtle — domain typosquats, urgency, money or credentials, and "do not tell anyone yet" framing.

Our standing policy is simple: forward suspicious messages to #security or use the "Report Phishing" button in our mail client. You never get in trouble for reporting something that turns out to be legitimate. You can get in trouble for clicking and not reporting.

Social engineering also happens by phone, Slack DM, and even in person ("I forgot my badge"). Apply the same instinct everywhere: an unusual urgent ask + a request to skip a normal control = report.
bullets: "Report Phishing" button is your default — speed beats certainty.
Urgency + money/credentials + secrecy = textbook phishing.
Verify out-of-band before you act on any urgent ask from an exec.
Vendor "support" emails asking for credentials are almost always fake.
Walk-in tailgating is social engineering too — challenge politely.

questions.prompt: What is the right first move?

choices.label: Wire the money — the CEO said it is urgent.
Reply to the email asking for verification.
Call/Slack the CEO on a known number, AND forward the email to #security.
Loop in finance privately and wait.

questions.scenario: Your CEO emails you at 11pm: "I'm in a board dinner — need you to wire $4,800 to a new vendor for tomorrow. Don't loop in finance, they're slow. I'll explain in the morning."

questions.prompt: Which of these are phishing red flags? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: The sender domain is "cloudanzen-support.com" instead of "cloudanzen.com".
The message demands action in the next hour.
The sender asks you to keep the request between just the two of you.
The email has correct grammar and a friendly tone.

questions.prompt: You accidentally clicked a link in a suspicious email. What do you do?

choices.label: Nothing — you did not enter credentials.
Report it in #security immediately with the email + URL details.
Wait a week to see if anything goes wrong.
Forward the link to a teammate to ask if it is safe.

modules.title: Secure development hygiene
modules.summary: Secrets, code review, dep updates, SSDLC.
modules.body:
If you ship code that touches customer data, your habits ARE the security control. The big four that move the needle: never commit secrets, every change goes through review, keep dependencies fresh, and write meaningful tests around security-sensitive logic.

We block secret commits in pre-commit hooks and CI, but pre-commit hooks fail occasionally and CI checks lag the push. If you commit a secret, rotate it (do not just remove the commit) and tell #security.

Code review is not just a quality gate — it is a control. Two pairs of eyes catch the "is this query rate-limited?" or "is this endpoint authenticated?" questions that nobody can catch alone at 6pm.
bullets: Never commit secrets — even in branches that "no one will see".
If a secret hits a repo, rotate it AND notify #security.
Every change goes through review with a thoughtful description.
Keep dependencies fresh; pay attention to Snyk / Dependabot PRs.
Write tests around auth + data-access boundaries.

questions.prompt: You realise you committed an API key in a feature branch yesterday. The branch is not merged. What do you do?

choices.label: Force-push to rewrite the commit and pretend it never happened.
Rotate the key immediately AND report it in #security.
Delete the branch — that removes the commit from GitHub.
Add the secret to .gitignore and re-commit.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong in a security-sensitive code review? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Is this endpoint authenticated AND authorized for the right role?
Are inputs validated against the documented schema?
Is there a sensible rate limit on the endpoint?
Did the author use tabs or spaces?

questions.prompt: What is the right move?

choices.label: Merge without reading — CI is green, Dependabot would not lie.
Read the linked advisory + changelog, then merge if it looks safe.
Close the PR — you have no time.
Reassign to the security team.

questions.scenario: A Dependabot PR opens for `acorn 8.9.0 → 8.11.3` flagged as a security update. The CI is green. Your sprint is full and you almost merge without reading anything.

modules.title: Vendor + cloud risk
modules.summary: New SaaS, OAuth approvals, DPA basics.
modules.body:
Every new SaaS we sign up for is a small extension of our security perimeter. A free trial of a productivity tool — innocent on the surface — can grant OAuth scopes that read your inbox or your customer documents. The vendor-onboarding workflow exists so we can evaluate that risk before the data starts flowing.

The shape is: open a #vendor-intake ticket with the use case, the data classes touched, and any contract URL. Security / legal review the DPA, sub-processors, and any AI training-data clauses. We approve, conditionally approve, or decline, and the result lives in the vendor inventory for the next review cycle.

OAuth approval prompts inside SaaS are a hidden vendor onboarding — same rules apply. If the prompt asks for "read all your Drive files" or "send mail on your behalf", do not click Accept without checking.
bullets: New vendor / new SaaS → open a #vendor-intake ticket first.
OAuth prompt requesting broad scopes is a vendor onboarding event.
Sub-processor changes from existing vendors require fresh review.
No DPA, no Customer Data. No exceptions.
Vendor risk reviews happen on a cadence — not just at intake.

questions.prompt: You want to start using a new AI meeting-notes tool. Free trial. It needs a Google Calendar OAuth that reads all events for the next year. What do you do first?

choices.label: Approve the OAuth — it is free, low-risk.
Open a #vendor-intake ticket with the use case and the OAuth scopes.
Use a personal Gmail to avoid the company exposure.
Wait and ask security if anyone else has used it.

questions.prompt: Which of these are real vendor-risk events that need review? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: A vendor adds a new sub-processor.
A vendor moves their hosting to a different region.
A vendor announces they will train AI on customer data unless we opt out.
A vendor sends us a Christmas card.

questions.prompt: What is the right move?

choices.label: Turn it on — sales already signed.
Open the standard #vendor-intake / integration review with the DPA + scope, even if it slows Friday.
Push back hard and refuse.
Ask the customer to do the security review.

questions.scenario: Sales pushes hard: "This customer wants us to integrate with their Snowflake. I already signed the DPA — can you turn it on by Friday?"

modules.title: Incidents + escalation
modules.summary: Recognise, escalate, preserve evidence.
modules.body:
An incident is anything that breaks — or could have broken — our security commitments. Not just attacks: a misrouted customer email, a leaked Slack invite, a deploy that exposed an unprotected endpoint, a vendor breach that touched our data. ISO 27001 Annex A.5.24 / A.5.26 / A.5.27 set the expectation that we handle these consistently.

Two things matter at first contact: speed and evidence. We have an on-call rotation; page it. Do not delete tickets, Slack threads, or screenshots — even if they are embarrassing. Evidence is what makes the postmortem meaningful and what protects us from claims later.

Postmortems are blameless. The point is the system fix, not the person. If you contributed to an incident, your most valuable action is being the most accurate witness in the postmortem.
bullets: When in doubt, declare an incident — under-declaration is worse than over-declaration.
Preserve evidence: no deleting tickets, threads, screenshots.
Page the on-call rotation, do not just DM your manager.
Blameless postmortems — the system is the target, not the person.
A near-miss is still worth a writeup.

questions.prompt: Rank these actions when you first suspect a real incident, from FIRST to LAST.

choices.label: Page the on-call security rotation.
Preserve evidence: no deleting tickets, threads, or screenshots.
Write a short timeline of what you saw and when.
Wait for instructions before taking remediation actions.

questions.prompt: Which of these count as security incidents we should declare? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: A customer report that received another customer's data in an export.
A teammate's managed laptop is stolen.
An accidental Slack thread sharing a partial customer email externally.
CI failed for an hour because of a transient AWS issue.

questions.prompt: After an incident, the postmortem identifies a process gap. The teammate involved feels personally responsible. What does the postmortem do with that?

choices.label: Cite the teammate in the writeup so others learn from the mistake.
Document the system fix; thank the teammate for accurate reporting.
Skip the postmortem to avoid awkwardness.
Punish the teammate quietly.

modules.title: Business continuity awareness
modules.summary: Backups, runbooks, the bus-factor question.
modules.body:
ISO 27001 Annex A.5.29 / A.5.30 covers what happens when something breaks — a database, a region, a vendor. The work is mostly done by infra and product engineering, but everyone contributes: keep runbooks current, document what you are the only one who knows, and treat tabletop exercises like real fire drills.

Backups are tested. Untested backups are a folk story. If you own a system, you own the periodic restore test that proves the backup actually works.

The hardest part of continuity is human, not technical. If only one teammate knows how the X service recovers, that is a single point of failure we should fix on a normal Tuesday — not at 3am when X is down.
bullets: Runbooks for what YOU own; keep them current; test them.
Backups are tested or they do not count.
Document the things only you know — that is the bus-factor risk.
Tabletop exercises matter; engage as if it were real.
Recovery is a team sport — keep the runbook simple enough that the on-call who has never seen it can run it.

questions.prompt: Your team's most critical database backs up nightly. The backup job is green for six months. Is the backup good?

choices.label: Yes — green for six months means it works.
Only if a recent restore actually succeeded.
Yes — the backup tool is from a reputable vendor.
No — backups never work; we should use replicas instead.

questions.prompt: You are the only person who knows how a critical service recovers. Which of these reduce the bus-factor risk? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Write a runbook with the exact commands + screenshots.
Walk a teammate through the runbook live.
Run a tabletop exercise where the teammate executes from the runbook alone.
Plan to do it after the launch — there is no time now.

questions.prompt: What is the right attitude?

choices.label: Skip — focus on real work.
Show up, engage as if real, file the gaps you find afterwards.
Show up but minimise effort.
Pretend the tabletop is happening but do not actually run it.

questions.scenario: A 2am tabletop exercise is announced for tomorrow. You think it is a low-priority exercise compared to real work.

modules.title: Audit + your role
modules.summary: What auditors ask, evidence habits, A.6.3 attestation.
modules.body:
ISO 27001 Annex A.6.3 says everyone with access to information assets gets relevant security awareness training. This course is one piece of that — your completion lands in our records as evidence the program is operating. Same idea applies to ISO 42001, SOC 2, HIPAA, NIST CSF: training records are real audit evidence.

When an auditor interviews you (it happens — they sample staff), the right move is to be honest, concise, and specific. Do not invent. "I do not know but I know who to ask" is a perfectly acceptable answer. Auditors prefer specificity over polish: "I report phishing using the button in our mail client" beats "we have a comprehensive phishing program".

Evidence is built every day, not the week before an audit. If you keep your tickets descriptive, your Slack threads searchable, and your access requests routed properly, the audit becomes a low-effort confirmation rather than an emergency reconstruction.
bullets: Your completed training is the A.6.3 evidence for you, personally.
"I do not know but I know who to ask" is fine.
Specific examples beat generic platitudes in an interview.
Evidence is built daily — not the week before the audit.
If you spot a gap during your normal work, file it — that IS the program.

questions.prompt: An auditor asks: "How do you report a suspicious email?" What is the best answer?

choices.label: We have a comprehensive phishing program.
I use the "Report Phishing" button in our mail client, and I have done so a few times this quarter.
I escalate via a centralised reporting workflow.
I would not know how.

questions.prompt: Which of these are healthy evidence habits during normal work? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Write descriptive Jira ticket titles, not "fix bug".
Capture approvals in the same Slack thread they were requested.
Link access requests to the role / project they are for.
Delete Slack threads after a sprint to keep things tidy.

questions.prompt: What is the right response?

choices.label: Make up a plausible answer.
Say "I do not know — that is owned by X / I would check with them".
Refuse to answer.
Defer to your manager only.

questions.scenario: An auditor asks you a question you genuinely do not know the answer to.

modules.title: What our AI policy means in practice
modules.summary: Why ISO 42001 exists and how it touches your daily work.
modules.body:
ISO 42001 is the new international standard for an AI Management System (AIMS). It is the AI counterpart to ISO 27001 — instead of asking "are you managing information securely?", it asks "are you managing your AI use responsibly?". For CloudAnzen, an AI-native product, getting this right is not optional: our customers, regulators, and auditors all want to know we are not shipping AI features by guess.

In practice, the AIMS shows up the same way the ISMS does — as policies, evidence we collect during normal work, and short reviews each quarter. The headline rules in our AI policy (A.2.2 objectives, A.2.3 resources, A.2.4 roles) translate to: we know what each AI feature is for, we have approved budget + tooling for it, and there is a named human owner.

You will not be asked to memorise the standard. You will be asked to recognise when an AI use is in-policy, when it is borderline, and when to pause and ask. That is the entire point of awareness training.
bullets: AI policy is the AIMS — controls, evidence, owners, reviews.
Every AI feature or workflow has a named human owner.
When in doubt about an AI use, ask in #ai-governance — silence is not a control.
Auditors sample real artefacts: prompts, model cards, approvals.
AI risk reviews happen before launch, not after an incident.

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes what the ISO 42001 AIMS is in practice at CloudAnzen?

choices.label: A one-time questionnaire that legal fills out.
The continuous operation around how we build, ship, and review AI — owners, approvals, prompts, model cards, reviews.
A switch we flip when we add an AI feature.
Only relevant to the data science team.

questions.prompt: Which of these are part of "the AIMS" in practice at CloudAnzen? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: The model card we publish for each shipped AI feature.
The Jira ticket where an AI feature got pre-launch risk-review approval.
The named human owner listed against each AI workflow in our AI inventory.
The ISO 42001 standard PDF sitting in a Drive folder.

questions.prompt: What is the right response?

choices.label: Agree — small features do not need review.
Encourage them to file the AI risk review; it is fast for low-risk and creates the evidence we need.
Refuse to help on the sprint.
Wait until launch and review afterwards.

questions.scenario: A PM proposes adding a new "AI summarisation" feature next sprint. They say it is small enough that they will skip the AI risk review and just ship it.

modules.title: Approved AI tools + acceptable use
modules.summary: Which AI tools are in-policy, and what counts as "use".
modules.body:
Our approved AI stack is documented in #ai-governance and in the AI Tool Register in Notion. The register lists which models, vendors, and SaaS AI features are allowed for which purposes, with the data classifications they are cleared for. If a tool is not on the register, treat it as not approved.

Acceptable use is shaped by three axes: the tool, the data sensitivity, and the task. A tool cleared for Internal data is not automatically cleared for Customer Data; an approved tool for code review is not automatically cleared for HR decisions. Our policy clauses A.9.2 (acceptable use) and A.9.4 (intended use) cover this — read them once.

Personal accounts, free tiers without a DPA, and "I just tried this new tool" all sit outside the AIMS. They are not banned outright, but they cannot be used for company work without going through the approval flow first.
bullets: Approved tools live in the AI Tool Register — check it before using a new tool.
Approval is per-tool AND per-data-classification AND per-task.
Personal accounts and free tiers without DPAs are not approved.
New tool to try? Open a request in #ai-governance — turnaround is days, not weeks.
Acceptable use is governed by A.9.2 / A.9.4 — read them once a year.

questions.prompt: Your friend at another company recommends a hot new code-review AI you have not heard of. You want to try it on a CloudAnzen pull request. What is the right move?

choices.label: Try it once on a small PR; one test is fine.
File a request in #ai-governance to add it to the AI Tool Register before using it on company code.
Use it from your personal account so it does not "count".
Use it on test data only with no review.

questions.prompt: Which of these are governed by A.9.2 acceptable use? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Pasting a sample customer support transcript into an approved LLM to draft a reply.
Asking an AI agent in the IDE to refactor a service that touches PII.
Building an AI feature into the product that classifies customer findings.
Reading an article on an LLM blog at lunch.

questions.prompt: Which actions are appropriate? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Use our approved enterprise LLM tier instead of the free one.
Paste only sections of the page that are already public.
Ask #ai-governance whether the use is in-policy.
Paste the full draft into the free LLM since it is "just wording".

questions.scenario: A teammate suggests using a popular free LLM chatbot to brainstorm wording for a customer-facing security trust-page. They want to paste a draft we have not published yet.

modules.title: Sensitive data in AI
modules.summary: What NEVER to paste, when to redact, when to escalate.
modules.body:
The fastest way to fail an audit and lose customers is to leak sensitive data into an AI model. AI vendors retain prompts and outputs for varying durations; some use them for training; some are subpoena-reachable. Treat every prompt as if it could appear in a regulator letter next year.

The hard rules: never paste raw Customer Data, credentials, secrets, or ePHI into any LLM — approved or otherwise — unless the workflow is explicitly cleared for it on the AI Tool Register. Redaction patterns help (placeholders for names, tokens, IDs) but they are a second line, not a license.

When you do need AI help on sensitive material, the answer is usually "use the approved enterprise tier with zero-retention contract terms, and redact aggressively". If you cannot remember the rules, the question to ask in #ai-governance is always faster than the cleanup after a leak.
bullets: Never paste raw secrets, tokens, or credentials into any AI tool.
Customer Data goes only into AI workflows cleared for that classification.
Redaction is a second line, not a license — start with "should this be in any AI at all?".
Zero-retention enterprise tiers are the right tool for sensitive AI work.
Vendor logs are subpoena-reachable for years. Plan accordingly.

questions.prompt: You have a stack trace from a customer bug report that includes the customer email + a partial API token. You want to ask an LLM to explain the error. What is the right approach?

choices.label: Paste the full stack trace as-is.
Redact the email AND the token (rotate the token if production), then ask in an approved tier.
Redact only the email; tokens are short enough to be safe.
Forward the whole report to a teammate to paste for you.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong in the "never paste into an LLM without explicit clearance" bucket? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: A production database connection string.
ePHI from a healthcare customer integration.
Unreleased quarterly revenue figures.
A made-up dummy dataset with no real customer mapping.

questions.prompt: What do you do?

choices.label: Paste it for them — it is internal-only and the email is going to the customer anyway.
Decline politely, point them at the approved enterprise tier + redaction guidelines, and offer to help.
Stay quiet — sales handles renewals.
Forward the request to the CEO.

questions.scenario: Sales wants to "spice up" a customer renewal email. They ask you to paste the customer's account-spend report and last three support tickets into a public LLM to generate "personalised" copy.

modules.title: AI risk + impact awareness
modules.summary: When a use needs the AI risk reviewer (and when it does not).
modules.body:
Not every AI use is high-risk. A teammate using an approved LLM to draft a Notion page is fine; the same teammate building an AI feature that auto-decides whether to alert a customer's on-call is not. ISO 42001 expects us to recognise the difference.

Our impact framework looks at three things: who the AI affects (just you? a teammate? a customer? a regulator?), how reversible the AI decision is (a draft you read = reversible; an auto-sent message = irreversible), and how visible the AI is to the affected party (could they tell AI was in the loop?).

Use cases that touch customers, are hard to reverse, or are invisible to the affected party MUST go through the AI risk reviewer before they ship. Use cases that are internal, reversible, and clearly AI-assisted can usually proceed under standard approved-tool guidance.
bullets: Three axes: who is affected, how reversible, how visible.
Customer-facing + irreversible + invisible = mandatory risk review.
Internal-only + reversible + visible = standard approved-tool path.
"Auto-decide" without a human in the loop is always high-risk.
When uncertain, the AI risk reviewer is a Slack ping away.

questions.prompt: Which of these AI use cases is most likely to need a formal AI risk review before shipping?

choices.label: You use an approved LLM to draft a Notion page about a feature spec.
A new feature that auto-decides which customers to email a renewal nudge to, and sends it without human review.
An AI code-review tool that suggests changes a human reviewer approves before merge.
A team experiment using an LLM to summarise public-blog data.

questions.prompt: Which of these characteristics PUSH an AI use case toward "high-risk"? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: The AI output directly affects a customer outside the company.
Once the AI acts, it is hard or impossible to reverse.
The affected party cannot tell that AI was used in the decision.
You use AI to summarise internal meeting notes you wrote yourself.

questions.prompt: What is the right next step?

choices.label: Run the A/B test — A/B testing is how we learn.
Pause the rollout, file the AI risk review, and add a human override path before any production test.
Run the test internally only.
Wait until launch and review afterwards.

questions.scenario: An engineer prototypes an AI feature that auto-classifies a customer security finding as "low" or "high" severity and routes accordingly. They want to A/B test it on real production data, with no human override path.

modules.title: Training + evaluation data
modules.summary: Provenance, licensing, bias screening — the everyone-version.
modules.body:
Most CloudAnzen teammates will never fine-tune a foundation model, but every team that builds AI features touches training or evaluation data in some form — prompt examples, eval sets, system-prompt seed data. Our AIMS expects each of those datasets to have a known provenance, a clear license to use, and a basic bias screening pass.

Provenance means "where did this data come from?". Public dataset? Internal synthetic data? Customer data with a contractual basis to use? Each has different downstream rules. Mixing them without recording which is which is the most common audit finding in this area.

Bias screening, even for small eval sets, is straightforward: look for class imbalance (one customer dominates the data), demographic imbalance (one language / region dominates), and outcome imbalance (the dataset only has "easy" cases). You do not need a PhD — you need a checklist and a teammate to spot-check.
bullets: Every eval / prompt / training dataset gets a provenance note.
Customer data in training only with a documented contractual basis.
Bias screening = class balance + demographic balance + outcome balance.
License + retention rules differ by data source — record them.
Synthetic data is fine but mark it as synthetic.

questions.prompt: You are putting together a 200-row eval set for a new AI feature. What is the first thing to record?

choices.label: The accuracy your model reaches on the set.
The provenance of each row — where it came from, license, sensitivity class.
Your gut on whether the data feels representative.
Nothing — it is just an eval set.

questions.prompt: Which of these are basic bias-screening checks for an eval set? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Does one customer or one source dominate the rows?
Does one language, region, or demographic dominate the rows?
Are all the rows "easy" cases where the right answer is obvious?
Are there at least 1,000 rows?

questions.prompt: What is the right response?

choices.label: Approve — we already have access to the tickets.
Pause; confirm the contractual basis to train on this customer's data, then check representativeness.
Pull the tickets but anonymise the customer name.
Refuse outright — training data is data-science-only.

questions.scenario: A teammate proposes pulling 500 random support tickets from a single customer to use as training examples for a new auto-reply AI, "since we already have them".

modules.title: Human oversight for high-risk AI
modules.summary: Override paths, escalation, and when "human in the loop" really means it.
modules.body:
"Human in the loop" is one of the most-misused phrases in AI. A human glancing at a list of AI-generated decisions before clicking "approve all" is not human oversight — it is rubber-stamping. ISO 42001 expects us to design real oversight: the human can actually inspect, override, and escalate.

For every high-risk AI feature, the design should answer three questions: how does a reviewer see what the AI decided, how do they reverse a single decision (not just stop the system), and how does a customer or affected party reach a human to dispute the AI outcome? If any of those answers is "they can't", the feature is not ready.

Override paths must actually work in production. A "kill switch" that has not been tested in six months is not a control — it is a hope. Drills are part of the AIMS.
bullets: Real oversight = can inspect, can override one decision, can escalate.
Rubber-stamping is not oversight — measure reviewer time and disagreement rate.
Customers and affected parties need a human escalation path.
Kill switches and override paths must be drilled.
"AI did it" is not a defence in an incident review.

questions.prompt: Which of these counts as meaningful human oversight under our AIMS?

choices.label: A reviewer who can see each AI decision, override any one of them, and escalate disputed ones.
A reviewer who sees the daily volume of AI decisions and clicks "approve all" once a day.
A kill switch that turns the entire AI feature off if something goes wrong.
An audit log no one reads.

questions.prompt: Which of these are signals that "human oversight" has degraded into rubber-stamping? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Reviewers spend less than a second per AI decision.
The override rate has been zero for months.
The reviewer UI only offers a "batch approve" button.
Reviewers occasionally override AI decisions and write notes.

questions.prompt: What does this tell you about the feature?

choices.label: Nothing — the kill switch is enough oversight.
The feature is missing required per-decision override; raise an AI risk review finding and add the control before the next release.
Tell the customer the AI made a final decision.
Pause the whole feature indefinitely.

questions.scenario: A customer disputes an AI-generated outcome on their account. The reviewer dashboard shows the decision, but there is no button to reverse just this one — only a "pause the whole feature" toggle.

modules.title: Vendor + foundation-model risk
modules.summary: DPAs, sub-processors, model lineage, version drift.
modules.body:
Almost every AI feature we ship rides on top of a foundation model from a vendor (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.). Each one is a sub-processor in our customer contracts, and each one has its own DPA, retention terms, and model-versioning policies. Pretending the vendor risk does not exist is the most common shortcut in AI shops our size.

For every AI vendor, three things matter: an active DPA, a documented data-flow (what data goes to them, with what retention), and a model-lineage record (which model version are we on, when did it change, what changed). The data-flow is more important than people expect — auditors ask about it constantly.

Model version drift is silent. A vendor can swap the underlying model under a stable name; behaviour changes; your eval results from last quarter no longer hold. Pinned versions, dated eval snapshots, and change-log monitoring are part of the AIMS.
bullets: Every AI vendor needs a DPA on file before production use.
Document the data flow: what goes to the vendor, retention, deletion path.
Pin model versions; do not chase the "latest" silently.
Re-run evals when a model version changes.
Update customer-facing sub-processor lists when AI vendors change.

questions.prompt: You are about to use a new foundation-model API in a production AI feature. Which of these MUST be in place first?

choices.label: A signed DPA on file.
Approval from the head of marketing.
A blog post explaining the feature.
A handshake with the vendor.

questions.prompt: Which of these are documented expectations for any AI vendor we use in production? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Signed DPA on file.
Documented data flow + retention terms.
Pinned model version + eval snapshot on each version change.
Customer testimonials about the vendor.

questions.prompt: What is the right reaction?

choices.label: Nothing — silent upgrades are usually improvements.
Pin the previous version if available, re-run evals, update the model card, then decide.
Disable the feature permanently.
Tell customers the model is now smarter.

questions.scenario: A vendor announces a "transparent" silent upgrade of their flagship model — same API name, "improved" behaviour. Your AI feature has been running on this model in production for months.

modules.title: AI incidents + reporting
modules.summary: Hallucination, biased output, prompt-injection in the wild.
modules.body:
AI incidents come in flavours that look different from classic security incidents: a model says something confidently wrong (hallucination), a model treats one demographic worse (bias), a model gets tricked by a hidden prompt in a customer file (prompt injection), or a model leaks data it should not have access to (extraction). All of these are reportable under our AIMS.

The reporting bar is the same as for security incidents: when in doubt, report. Use #ai-governance for non-urgent, page the on-call for live customer impact. Include the model + version, the prompt or input that triggered it (sanitised), and what happened. The AI-incident log is the artefact auditors review.

Reporting fast matters most when there is customer impact: an AI feature that emails the wrong customer, classifies a finding incorrectly, or exposes data is a real incident. "It is just an AI hiccup" is not a defensible response.
bullets: Hallucination + bias + prompt injection + data extraction are all AI incidents.
Customer impact = page the on-call; non-urgent = #ai-governance.
Sanitise any data in the report before pasting.
AI incident log is real audit evidence — fill it out properly.
When in doubt: report. Same rule as security.

questions.prompt: You discover an AI feature in production is occasionally emailing the wrong customer their own data. Rank these actions from FIRST to LAST.

choices.label: Page the on-call to disable the affected feature path.
File the AI incident report with model + version + sanitised inputs.
Notify affected customers per the incident comms plan.
Schedule the postmortem and queue the fix.

questions.prompt: Which of these count as AI incidents under our AIMS? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: A confidently-wrong AI answer that a customer acted on.
An AI feature that returns systematically worse results for one demographic.
A customer-uploaded document that contained a hidden prompt and changed the AI behaviour.
A teammate complaining the model is "dumb today" with no customer impact.

questions.prompt: You suspect prompt injection — an AI feature is reading text from customer files and the output suggests it executed instructions embedded in a file. What is the right first step?

choices.label: Test it on more customer files yourself to confirm.
Report immediately to #security and #ai-governance; pause the feature path while it is investigated.
Ignore — prompt injection is just a theoretical risk.
Post the suspicious file content in #general for discussion.

modules.title: Transparency + customer disclosure
modules.summary: When to tell the customer AI is in the loop.
modules.body:
Customers increasingly expect to know when AI is involved in a decision that affects them. ISO 42001 frames this as a transparency obligation — and several jurisdictions (EU AI Act, NYC Local Law 144, others) are turning that expectation into law. Our policy is to be transparent by default.

Three rules cover most cases: tell the customer when AI directly affects their account (auto-decisions, generated content sent to them), include AI vendors in our public sub-processor list, and give customers a path to ask a human about an AI outcome. Those three together cover the bulk of regulatory and audit expectations.

Internal AI use (drafting, summarising, code-review) does not always need customer-level disclosure but should be disclosed in our trust-center under "how we use AI". The bar is "could the customer reasonably want to know?".
bullets: AI that directly affects a customer outcome = disclose to the customer.
AI vendors that touch customer data = public sub-processor list.
Customers can always reach a human about an AI outcome.
Internal AI use goes in the trust-center "how we use AI" section.
When uncertain, disclose. Transparency is a feature, not a tax.

questions.prompt: A new AI feature auto-suggests an answer in a customer-facing chat widget. The customer can accept, edit, or ignore the suggestion. Does the customer need to know AI is involved?

choices.label: No — a human edits it before sending.
Yes — disclose with a label or pattern (e.g. "AI-drafted, human-reviewed").
Only if the customer asks.
Only if the law in their jurisdiction requires it.

questions.prompt: Which of these are standard transparency artefacts at CloudAnzen? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: The public sub-processor list updated when AI vendors change.
The "how we use AI" page in the trust-center.
In-product labelling that flags AI-generated content.
A secret internal Notion page about which features use AI.

questions.prompt: What is the lesson for the AIMS?

choices.label: Customers should not assume any reply is human-written.
Disclosure is cheap up front; cleanup is expensive after the fact. Add labelling + update the playbook.
Tell the customer "all of our replies are AI now".
Block the customer for complaining.

questions.scenario: A customer support agent sends a customer an AI-drafted reply without labelling it. The customer later discovers it was AI-generated and complains they were "talking to a bot".

modules.title: Model card + records discipline
modules.summary: What we keep, where, why auditors love it.
modules.body:
A model card is a one-page (or few-page) record of what an AI feature is, what it is for, what it is NOT for, who owns it, which model version it uses, when it was last evaluated, and how it can be turned off. Every AI feature we ship to customers has one. Every internal AI workflow that touches Confidential or Customer Data has one.

Auditors love model cards because they answer the questions they would otherwise have to ask in long meetings: what does this thing do, who decided it should exist, how do we know it works, who is accountable. A current model card is worth ten paragraphs of "trust us".

Records discipline means the model cards do not rot. Quarterly review (or on every material change — new model version, new dataset, new failure mode) keeps them honest. A model card that has not been touched in 18 months is a finding.
bullets: Every customer-facing or sensitive AI feature has a current model card.
Model card answers: what, who, version, eval, off-switch.
Quarterly review or on material change — whichever comes first.
Out-of-date cards are findings, not "minor housekeeping".
Model cards are public-friendly: most of them go in the trust-center.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs on a model card?

choices.label: A marketing tagline.
Named owner, intended use, non-uses, model version, last eval, off-switch.
The engineer's favourite quote.
A cost spreadsheet only.

questions.prompt: Which of these trigger a model-card review? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: A new model version from the vendor.
A new dataset added to training or evaluation.
A new failure mode observed in production.
The named owner is on holiday for a week.

questions.prompt: What is the right move in the moment AND afterwards?

choices.label: Tell the auditor the card "is being updated as we speak".
Acknowledge the staleness as a finding, commit to a remediation date, follow up in writing.
Refuse to show the card.
Edit the model card in front of the auditor.

questions.scenario: An auditor asks you in a walkthrough: "show me the model card for your AI risk-classifier and tell me when it was last reviewed". You open the card and it was last touched 14 months ago.

modules.title: Customer trust at CloudAnzen
modules.summary: What SOC 2 is, from a builder's perspective.
modules.body:
SOC 2 is the audit report enterprise buyers ask for when they want independent confirmation that we operate the way we say we do. It is organised around five Trust Services Criteria (TSC): Security (mandatory), Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, and Privacy. CloudAnzen reports against Security, Availability, and Confidentiality today; Privacy and Processing Integrity are on the roadmap.

Unlike ISO 27001 (which certifies the management system), a SOC 2 audit is the auditor sampling your controls over a window (a "Type 1" is point-in-time; a "Type 2" is over 3–12 months). The auditor reads our control descriptions, then pulls real samples to confirm each one actually operated. Your day-to-day work is the evidence pool.

The mental model: every commitment we make to a customer in a contract or trust-center page eventually becomes a control in our SOC 2 description. The auditor checks the control. So the controls you follow on Monday morning are the report the customer reads next year.
bullets: SOC 2 covers Security (always) + selected Availability / Confidentiality / Processing Integrity / Privacy.
Type 1 = point in time; Type 2 = a window. We aim for Type 2.
Auditors sample controls — your real work is the sample pool.
Customer commitments → controls → audit evidence; all one chain.
No "audit binder" — continuous evidence is the entire game.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the relationship between SOC 2 and your daily work at CloudAnzen?

choices.label: SOC 2 is a separate compliance project the security team owns.
Your everyday tickets, approvals, and reviews become the audit evidence the auditor samples.
SOC 2 evidence is produced retroactively the week before the audit.
SOC 2 is for sales decks; engineering does not need to think about it.

questions.prompt: Which of these are Trust Services Criteria covered by SOC 2? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Security
Availability
Confidentiality
Profitability

questions.prompt: What do you tell them?

choices.label: Promise the Type 2 — close the deal first, audit later.
Explain the audit window requirement; offer interim evidence under NDA (Type 1, questionnaire, pen-test summary) and a target date for Type 2.
Refuse to engage with sales.
Tell sales to "make something up".

questions.scenario: Sales asks if we can "throw together" a SOC 2 Type 2 report for a deal closing in two weeks.

modules.title: Confidentiality + customer data
modules.summary: How we keep customer data out of places it should not be.
modules.body:
The Confidentiality TSC is mostly about three things: who can see customer data, where customer data can live, and how it gets disposed of. Most SOC 2 audit findings in this area are not exotic — they are "a former contractor still had access" or "a prod export ended up in a personal Drive".

Our hard rules: customer data lives only in approved systems (the product database, the data warehouse with row-level access, S3 buckets with encryption + access logs). It never lives in someone's personal cloud, in a screenshot in a public Slack channel, or in a CSV downloaded "just to check something".

When a teammate leaves, the de-provisioning checklist is the single most important control. Auditors will pull samples of leaver tickets and confirm every system was revoked within SLA. A missed revocation is a finding; a pattern of missed revocations is a qualification.
bullets: Customer data lives only in approved systems — never personal drives.
Downloads / exports of customer data are themselves auditable events.
Leaver de-provisioning is the most-sampled control in this area.
Public Slack channels are not "internal" — they leak.
Encryption at rest + in transit is table stakes, not the whole answer.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the most common SOC 2 confidentiality finding for companies our size?

choices.label: Encryption keys being too short.
A former employee or contractor whose access was not fully revoked within SLA.
A customer's data being too encrypted.
A misconfigured DNS record.

questions.prompt: Which of these handlings are in-policy for customer data? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Querying the approved data warehouse with row-level access controls.
Read-only ephemeral access via the approved tool for a 1-hour debug session.
Exporting a customer CSV to your personal Google Drive.
Sharing a logged, audited export with a teammate through the approved channel.

questions.prompt: What is the right answer?

choices.label: Sure, a few days is fine.
No — access ends on the last day. Any wrap-up needs to happen before or through documented arrangements.
Let them keep access but ask them not to commit anything.
Stay silent and let it sort itself out.

questions.scenario: A teammate gives notice. Their last day is Friday. They ask you on Thursday afternoon whether they can "keep their GitHub access for a few days after to wrap things up".

modules.title: Availability + incident discipline
modules.summary: What "uptime" really means in a SOC 2 report.
modules.body:
Availability covers our commitment that the product is reachable when customers need it. It is not the same as a 100% uptime promise — it is about whether we have the right controls (monitoring, on-call, capacity planning, runbooks, postmortems) to detect and recover from outages within our stated SLOs.

For SOC 2, auditors sample three things: incident records (do we open one when something breaks, is it timely, does it have severity + impact + actions?), monitoring evidence (did the alert fire, did someone acknowledge it, did the page reach the right person?), and recovery / DR drills (do we actually test backups and failover?).

The dangerous habit to avoid is the "no incident" incident — when the system is degraded but nobody opens a ticket because "it was just a blip". If it was customer-visible, it is an incident; not opening the ticket is a finding.
bullets: Availability ≠ 100% uptime; it is controls + SLO compliance.
Customer-visible degradation = open the incident, every time.
Monitoring evidence (alert fired, ack, page chain) is sampled.
DR / backup drills are not optional — they must actually run.
"Just a blip" is the most common audit gap in availability.

questions.prompt: Mid-afternoon: a 12-minute partial degradation affects ~5% of customers. The on-call resolves it without opening an incident "because it was so short". What is the SOC 2 implication?

choices.label: No implication — incidents under 15 minutes do not count.
A finding — customer-visible degradation requires an incident record regardless of duration. Open it retroactively with timeline.
Only a finding if the SLO was breached.
Send the on-call home and forget about it.

questions.prompt: Which of these are sampled by SOC 2 auditors under the Availability TSC? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Incident records with severity, impact, and timeline.
Monitoring + alert acknowledgement evidence.
Postmortem documents with action items.
Marketing analytics dashboard screenshots.

questions.prompt: What is the right move?

choices.label: Skip it; nobody will know.
Either run a scoped version on Tuesday OR formally defer with a documented exception + new date.
Move the drill to next year.
Cancel all future drills.

questions.scenario: A DR backup-restore drill is scheduled for next Tuesday but the team is slammed with a launch. Someone suggests skipping the drill this quarter and "running two next quarter".

modules.title: Processing integrity + change discipline
modules.summary: Changes go through review, every time.
modules.body:
Processing Integrity is our commitment that the system processes data the way it is supposed to — completely, accurately, on time, and authorised. In a SaaS context, the practical translation is "every change to production goes through a documented review with the right approver, and we can prove it".

For SOC 2, the auditor will pull a sample of recent changes (PRs, infra changes, schema migrations) and check: was there a ticket, was there a review by someone other than the author, was there evidence the change was tested, was the deploy logged. The control is simple; the failures are usually around emergency / hotfix paths where the discipline gets skipped.

The hotfix / emergency path needs its own paper trail. "We had to ship fast" is not an excuse to skip review forever — the hotfix policy should have a documented after-the-fact review + signoff so the change still gets a second pair of eyes, even if late.
bullets: Every production change has a ticket, a reviewer, and a deploy log.
Self-review does not satisfy "review by someone other than the author".
Hotfix path has its own documented after-the-fact review.
Schema migrations are changes too — same controls apply.
"Move fast" + "break the control" = audit finding.

questions.prompt: Which of these counts as evidence of a properly-reviewed production change?

choices.label: A self-merged PR with a green CI run.
A PR linked to a ticket, reviewed and approved by a non-author, with a deploy log entry.
A Slack message saying "looks good".
A change with no ticket but a long commit message.

questions.prompt: Which of these are considered "changes" under our processing-integrity controls? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: A code PR that ships behaviour changes.
A Terraform / infra change.
A feature-flag flip that changes behaviour for real customers.
Updating your profile picture in the internal directory.

questions.prompt: What is the right follow-up for SOC 2 evidence?

choices.label: Nothing — emergency hotfix is exempt from review forever.
Open the hotfix ticket + after-the-fact review + signoff within the defined SLA so the change has a documented second reviewer.
Quietly close the deploy log entry.
Punish the on-call for skipping review.

questions.scenario: A live outage forces a same-minute hotfix. The on-call self-merges and ships it without a reviewer. The customer impact is fixed in 4 minutes.

modules.title: Evidence habits
modules.summary: Tickets, approvals, dashboards — make them audit-friendly by default.
modules.body:
The single biggest difference between companies that pass SOC 2 in one go and companies that get qualified findings is the quality of their everyday evidence trail. The fix is not "produce more evidence at audit time" — it is "make the evidence we already produce more useful".

Three habits matter most: every state-changing action gets a ticket (not a DM, not a verbal nod); every approval is given in writing on the artefact itself (the PR, the ticket, the change request), not in a side channel; and the dashboards we use to monitor the system live in a known place and are referenced from the runbook.

A teammate-to-future-teammate test is useful: if you left tomorrow, could the next person reconstruct what happened from the artefacts alone? If the answer is "only if they DM the right person", the evidence trail is not audit-ready.
bullets: State-changing action → ticket. Not a DM.
Approvals on the artefact (PR, ticket, change request), not in DM.
Dashboards live in known places, linked from runbooks.
"Future teammate" test: can someone reconstruct without DMs?
Audit evidence quality compounds — invest weekly, not yearly.

questions.prompt: Your manager DMs "approved" for a change request. What is the right next step for SOC 2 evidence?

choices.label: Screenshot the DM for the audit file.
Ask the manager to post the approval on the ticket or PR itself, so it is on the artefact.
Accept the DM and move on.
Forward the DM to the whole company.

questions.prompt: Rank these evidence forms for an approval from STRONGEST to WEAKEST.

choices.label: A written approval comment on the PR or change ticket itself.
A Slack message in a documented channel referencing the change.
A direct message between two people.
A verbal "go for it" in a hallway conversation.

questions.prompt: Which of these patterns help future-you survive an audit sample? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Linking every PR to a ticket.
Referencing the runbook in incident records.
Writing decisions down in a durable doc, not just Slack.
Keeping all approvals in 1:1 DMs only.

modules.title: Monitoring + on-call
modules.summary: What alerts mean, how escalation actually works.
modules.body:
Monitoring + on-call is where Availability and Incident Response controls meet reality. SOC 2 expects we have monitoring that fires on the things we said we would monitor (per our control description), that pages reach the right person, that acknowledgements happen within stated SLAs, and that escalation chains kick in when nobody acknowledges.

The most common audit gaps in this area are not technical — they are about discipline. Stale on-call rotations (someone left, nobody updated the rotation), alerts that page nobody (false-positives muted permanently, the muting forgotten), and SLA breaches with no record of why nobody answered.

Your part: if you are on-call, acknowledge promptly even if you cannot fix immediately. If you receive a page that should not have routed to you, escalate before you sleep on it. The page-chain evidence is what auditors sample.
bullets: Page → ack within SLA, even if fix is later.
Stale rotations are the most common on-call audit gap.
Muting alerts is fine — undocumented muting is a finding.
Escalation chain must actually fire when ack is missed.
If a page mis-routed, escalate to fix the routing, do not just absorb it.

questions.prompt: You ack a page at 2am but cannot start fixing it until your shift partner wakes up. What does SOC 2 expect?

choices.label: Ignore the page until morning.
Ack within SLA, then either start the fix or escalate to your partner / next-in-rotation with handoff notes.
Mute the alert and go back to bed.
Disable monitoring on the affected service.

questions.prompt: Which of these on-call patterns produce audit findings? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: On-call rotation still lists a teammate who left 3 months ago.
An alert was muted last sprint with no ticket or rationale.
Three pages went unacked last quarter with no follow-up.
Weekly on-call handover with documented hot-spots.

questions.prompt: What is the right first action?

choices.label: Ignore the page; it was not really for you.
Ack the page, route it to the correct on-call if there is impact, then fix the rotation the next business day with a documented change.
Forward to the leaver's personal email.
Disable the page entirely.

questions.scenario: You inherit on-call from a teammate who left. The Pagerduty schedule still lists them. You get paged at 3am for something irrelevant to you.

modules.title: Vendor + sub-processor awareness
modules.summary: Our vendors are our customers' vendors too.
modules.body:
Every SaaS we use that touches customer data is a sub-processor under our customer contracts. Customers expect to see those sub-processors on our public sub-processor list, with DPAs on file, and they expect to be notified before we add new ones. SOC 2 expects the same controls plus evidence we vet vendors before onboarding and review them periodically.

The right path for adding a new vendor: file a request in the vendor-onboarding queue with the data the vendor will touch, the data classification, and the use case. Security + legal review, DPA signed, sub-processor list updated, customer notification sent if required. Trying to "just try" a vendor before review is the most common audit gap here.

Existing vendors get periodic re-review (typically annual) on three axes: is the SOC 2 / ISO report current, has the data flow changed, has the vendor had any reported incidents. A stale vendor review for a critical vendor is a finding.
bullets: Every vendor touching customer data is a sub-processor — public list.
New vendor → onboarding request → DPA → list update → customer notify.
No "just trying" a vendor with real customer data.
Annual review: SOC 2 / ISO current, data flow, vendor incidents.
Vendor offboarding has the same discipline as leaver offboarding.

questions.prompt: Marketing wants to try a new email-sending vendor with our customer list for a quick campaign. What is the right path?

choices.label: Run the campaign first, paper the vendor later.
File vendor onboarding (DPA, SOC 2 / ISO check), update sub-processor list, notify customers per policy, then send.
Use the new vendor with a small subset to test.
Manually export the list and paste into the vendor UI.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong on the public sub-processor list? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: The cloud provider hosting the product database.
The product-analytics vendor ingesting customer interactions.
The customer-support platform handling tickets.
The internal HR system used only by CloudAnzen staff.

questions.prompt: What is the right first move under SOC 2 + our contracts?

choices.label: Wait for the vendor to send us a full report.
Open an incident, assess customer data exposure, notify affected customers within the contractual window, update the vendor risk record.
Do nothing publicly; tell only the head of sales.
Switch vendors immediately without telling anyone.

questions.scenario: A vendor we depend on for a critical feature announces they were breached, with potential exposure of customer data we sent them.

modules.title: Auditor walkthrough — your part
modules.summary: What to expect when an auditor asks you for evidence.
modules.body:
When the SOC 2 auditor is on-site (virtually or otherwise), they will ask owners of sampled controls to walk through how the control operates. This is normal, healthy, and your part is to be calm and accurate. Your job is not to "convince" the auditor — your job is to show how the control actually works.

The shape of a walkthrough: the auditor asks "show me how X works", you open the system, you do the thing, you show the resulting evidence (ticket, log line, dashboard). If there is a gap, name it — gaps caught and disclosed are smaller findings than gaps the auditor finds themselves.

"I don't know" is a fine answer if it's followed with "let me find the right owner". Making things up to look helpful is the single most damaging thing you can do in a walkthrough — auditors recognise improvisation immediately.
bullets: Walkthroughs are demonstrations, not interrogations.
"I don't know — let me get the right owner" is always acceptable.
Never improvise or guess; that turns minor findings into major ones.
Self-disclosed gaps are smaller findings than auditor-discovered ones.
Pre-audit dry-runs save weeks of post-audit pain.

questions.prompt: An auditor asks to see evidence of a control and you genuinely do not know where it is. What is the right response?

choices.label: Make up a plausible answer to look helpful.
Say "I do not know the specifics — let me get the owner who does" and follow up promptly.
Refuse to answer.
Send the auditor away.

questions.prompt: Which of these reduce audit pain and follow-up findings? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Running a pre-audit dry-run of likely walkthroughs.
Self-disclosing known gaps with a remediation plan attached.
Keeping evidence on the artefact, not in DMs.
Improvising on the spot if asked something unfamiliar.

questions.prompt: What is the right move?

choices.label: Hide it and hope the auditor does not notice.
Disclose the mismatch with the evidence; agree to update the report description after the audit.
Change the control to match the description on the spot.
Stop doing the control entirely.

questions.scenario: During a walkthrough you realise the control description in our SOC 2 report does not quite match what we actually do — the documented frequency says monthly but we actually do it weekly.

modules.title: PHI + ePHI — what counts
modules.summary: What counts as protected health information, and what does not.
modules.body:
PHI (Protected Health Information) is any information about a person's health, healthcare, or healthcare payment that can be linked back to them. ePHI is the same thing but stored or transmitted electronically. Almost everything we touch in a healthcare-customer integration is ePHI.

The HIPAA "18 identifiers" rule is worth knowing roughly: names, addresses below state level, dates more granular than year, phone, email, SSN, MRN, account numbers, IP addresses, biometric IDs, photos, and so on. Combine ANY of those with health info and you have PHI.

The trap most newcomers fall into: thinking "I removed the name, so it is not PHI". De-identification is a specific process with strict rules. A zip code + birthdate + diagnosis is still identifiable (literally 87% of US residents can be uniquely identified by that triplet). When in doubt, treat it as PHI.
bullets: PHI = health info that can be linked back to a person.
ePHI = the same but stored or transmitted electronically.
There are 18 identifiers — combinations make it identifiable too.
"I removed the name" is not the same as de-identified.
When in doubt, treat as PHI.

questions.prompt: Which of these is PHI?

choices.label: A general marketing newsletter subscriber email list.
A note in a customer support ticket saying "patient John D. was admitted for cardiac care on 2026-03-15".
A count of "1,243 patients used the feature this month" with no identifiers.
Your teammate's personal yoga-class calendar invite.

questions.prompt: Which of these can re-identify a person even after the obvious name is removed? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Zip code + date of birth + sex.
A high-resolution face photo.
A free-text clinical note that quotes the patient verbatim.
Truncated patient initials with no other context.

questions.prompt: Is this in-policy?

choices.label: Yes — removing names is sufficient.
No — use the Safe Harbor method (remove all 18 identifiers), Expert Determination, or synthetic data.
Yes, if the demo is internal-only.
Yes, if it is just for screenshots.

questions.scenario: A teammate wants to use customer ePHI in a demo. They say they'll "remove the names" first.

modules.title: Minimum necessary access
modules.summary: Touch only the PHI you actually need to do your job.
modules.body:
The HIPAA Privacy Rule's minimum-necessary standard says: when you use, disclose, or request PHI, limit it to the minimum amount needed to do the task. For us this translates to: do not query whole patient datasets when you only need one row, do not export when reading on-screen is enough, and do not keep PHI longer than you need.

Our access model implements this with row-level access in the warehouse, scoped query templates, and time-bound debugging access. Standing broad access to PHI is exactly what HIPAA expects us not to have — and what auditors look for.

When you debug a customer issue, the right question to ask before opening the data is "what is the smallest subset I need to confirm or fix this?". The answer is almost always smaller than "the whole table".
bullets: Touch the smallest PHI subset needed for the task.
No standing broad-access roles for PHI.
Time-bound debugging access > permanent grants.
Reading on-screen > exporting; exporting > downloading.
Delete debug copies of PHI when done.

questions.prompt: You're debugging a single customer's issue. The warehouse offers two views: "all patients in their org" and "just the affected patient". Which do you use?

choices.label: "All patients in their org" — just in case I need context.
"Just the affected patient" — minimum necessary.
Whichever is faster to load.
Download the entire dataset to a local file.

questions.prompt: Which of these are in-policy ways to give a teammate temporary PHI access for debugging? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Time-bound JIT grant via the access management tool.
Scoped read-only view limited to the affected patient.
Pair-debugging on your existing session with full audit log.
Sharing your own login credentials.

questions.prompt: What is the right response?

choices.label: Grant the permanent access.
Decline; offer to improve the JIT-grant flow so debugging is fast without permanent access.
Ignore the request.
Grant for "just one quarter".

questions.scenario: A teammate asks for permanent read access to all customer PHI "so I do not have to keep asking for grants every time I debug something".

modules.title: Secure communication
modules.summary: Email, Slack, ticketing, screen-share — where PHI is OK.
modules.body:
Communication tools are where ePHI most commonly leaks accidentally. The HIPAA Security Rule expects us to encrypt ePHI in transit, control which tools handle it, and audit access. In practice that means: PHI goes only through tools we have a BAA with, never through DM-tier personal apps, and screen-sharing on PHI is treated like a recording event.

Our approved comms stack for PHI: the support platform (BAA on file), encrypted email with the healthcare label, and the patient-context channels in the support tool. Slack DMs, regular email, screenshots in #general, and personal SMS are all out of scope.

Screen-sharing during demos or pair-debugging is the most-forgotten leak vector. Before you share your screen, close PHI tabs, blur or mask the patient ID column, and announce "I am sharing — anything sensitive on screen?" before clicking share.
bullets: PHI only through BAA-covered tools.
Slack DMs / regular email / personal SMS = not approved for PHI.
Screen-share = recording event — close PHI tabs first.
Screenshots of PHI follow the same rules as the original.
When you must send PHI, use the approved encrypted path.

questions.prompt: A customer support agent needs to share patient details with engineering to debug a bug. Which channel is in-policy?

choices.label: Slack DM the engineer with a quick screenshot.
The patient-context channel in the support platform (BAA on file).
Personal SMS to the engineer.
Email without the healthcare-encrypted label.

questions.prompt: You're about to share your screen in a demo. Which checks should you do first? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Close any tabs showing PHI.
Mask or blur patient identifier columns.
Disable Slack / email notifications during the share.
Share the whole desktop without checking what is open.

questions.prompt: What do you do?

choices.label: Keep going and hope nobody noticed.
Stop sharing immediately, acknowledge it, report as a HIPAA-adjacent incident with the timeline.
Quickly close the tab without saying anything.
Ask the prospects to forget what they saw.

questions.scenario: You realise mid-screen-share that a tab with a patient's name and diagnosis is visible. Three customer prospects are on the call.

modules.title: Workstation + device safeguards
modules.summary: The laptop that touches PHI has stricter rules.
modules.body:
The HIPAA Security Rule has a whole section on workstation security. Any device that touches ePHI needs disk encryption, screen-lock, MDM, and tightly-managed software. Personal devices touching PHI are a category we avoid entirely — the policy bias is that PHI work happens on managed laptops only.

Three habits matter most on a PHI-touching laptop: screen-lock every time you step away (yes, even in your home office), keep ePHI out of local downloads / desktop / personal cloud sync, and report a lost or stolen device within the hour so MDM can remote-wipe.

BYOD with PHI is essentially never approved. Even temporary BYOD for an emergency requires explicit security signoff and a documented exception. The audit consequence of an unmanaged device touching PHI is severe.
bullets: PHI work happens on managed laptops only.
Screen-lock every single time — even at home.
No local downloads / desktop / personal cloud sync of PHI.
Lost / stolen device with PHI = page #security within the hour.
BYOD with PHI is essentially never approved.

questions.prompt: You have to debug a PHI issue urgently and your work laptop is at the office. Your personal laptop is right here. What is the right move?

choices.label: Use the personal laptop "just this once".
Wait, hand off to a teammate with a managed laptop, OR get explicit security signoff for a documented exception.
Forward the PHI to your personal email.
Use your phone's personal browser.

questions.prompt: Which of these are required workstation safeguards on a PHI-touching laptop? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Full-disk encryption enabled.
Screen lock that auto-engages quickly when idle.
MDM enrolled with remote-wipe capability.
Custom wallpaper.

questions.prompt: What is the right first action?

choices.label: Wait until you get home to look properly.
Page #security right now so MDM can remote-lock + wipe and open the incident.
Tell your manager only.
Buy a new laptop.

questions.scenario: You realise on the train that your work laptop — which has had PHI on it this morning — is no longer in your bag.

modules.title: BAA awareness
modules.summary: When our customers are covered entities, and what changes.
modules.body:
A Business Associate Agreement (BAA) is the contract that makes us a "Business Associate" under HIPAA when a customer is a Covered Entity (typically a healthcare provider, health plan, or clearinghouse). Without a BAA, we cannot legally process their PHI; with one, we take on direct HIPAA obligations including breach notification.

For you in day-to-day work: check whether a customer is BAA-covered before you treat their data as PHI. If yes, every interaction with their data follows the PHI rules in this course. If no but health-adjacent, escalate to legal — the answer is rarely "we can paste it anywhere".

Our sub-processors (cloud providers, support tools, analytics) that touch PHI must each have BAAs with us. When a new AI vendor or SaaS is proposed for healthcare data, "do they have a BAA?" is one of the first three questions. If they cannot offer one, the path is closed.
bullets: BAA = the contract that puts us under HIPAA as a Business Associate.
Check customer BAA status before treating their data as PHI.
Sub-processors touching PHI need BAAs too.
"No BAA" from a vendor = path closed for healthcare workloads.
When in doubt about BAA scope, legal owns the question.

questions.prompt: A new healthcare customer onboards. Engineering is asked to build a custom integration with the customer's EMR.

choices.label: Start coding immediately; BAA can come later.
Confirm the BAA is signed before any production / real-PHI work begins; use synthetic data until then.
Use real PHI in staging "to be realistic".
Refuse to engage until legal sends a memo.

questions.prompt: Which of these are HIPAA-relevant questions to ask before onboarding a new vendor for a healthcare workload? (pick all that apply)

choices.label: Will they sign a BAA?
Encryption at rest + in transit + audit logging?
HITRUST / SOC 2 + HIPAA mapping?
What kind of snacks does their office serve?

questions.prompt: What is the right path?

choices.label: Use the vendor anyway with "anonymised" PHI.
